items.summary: A study demonstrates that adding an auxiliary uncertainty signal to large language model decisions enhances their reliability in screening titles and abstracts for systematic reviews, addressing the need for more calibrated uncertainty in LLM-assisted research. items.summary: The study examines how large language models (LLMs) and humans process repeated words, finding that LLMs may either reactivate prior knowledge or re-evaluate each word anew, while post-training modifications can alter these behaviors. The findings could have broader implications for understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying language comprehension in both artificial and natural systems.

items.title: Which Question Is Your Attention Metric Answering? Attention Rows as Compositional Data
items.description:
arXiv:2608.14712v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Each row of a transformer's attention matrix is a probability distribution over tokens, and in trained models most of that probability lands on a single \emph{sink} token, usually the first. Standard tools for comparing attention rows (cosine similari
items.summary: Researchers have found that in most transformer models, attention rows primarily focus on a single "sink" token, typically the first one, indicating a bias in how attention is distributed. This finding matters because standard methods for analyzing these distributions may not effectively capture the true nature of attention mechanisms, highlighting the need for new tools to better understand them.
items.summary_detailed: Researchers have discovered that in many transformer models, each row of the attention matrix predominantly focuses on a single "sink" token, typically the first one. This finding has sparked debate among experts regarding how to accurately compare and interpret these attention rows using standard tools like cosine similarity. The broader impact could reshape our understanding of how language models process information and potentially influence future model design and evaluation methods.
items.summary_bullets:
• Each attention row in transformers is a probability distribution.
• Most probability in attention rows focuses on a single "sink" token.
• Sink tokens are typically the first token in the sequence.
• Standard comparison tools like cosine similarity may not be effective.
